land.text: Youzhou, the former Yan core round modern Beijing, left to the Yan general Li Huaixian

predecessors.note: An Lushan rebellion page: 'Li Huaixian was made military governor (jiedushi) of Lulong Circuit, headquartered in modern Beijing and covering Youzhou, the former Yan core'.

land.text: the Lulong circuit, which Liu Shouguang made the Yan in 911 (Prince of Yan 910), with Cang Prefecture taken in 910

successors.note: Liu Rengong retired under Later Liang in 910; the Yan fell to Jin in late 913. Cang (Yichang) fell to Liu Shouguang in 910 and goes with the circuit.

capitals.name: You Prefecture (Youzhou, Beijing)
capitals.note: 'Headquartered in modern Beijing'; You Prefecture is the Lulong capital on the Liu Rengong page.

correction.text: the Lulong circuit round You Prefecture (Youzhou), 'near present-day Beijing': the Yan Kingdom shape of 911 stands for the circuit, with Ying (Hejian) and Mo (Renqiu) south of it

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. The An Lushan page names You Prefecture (modern Beijing) as the headquarters and gives no frontier or area. The Yan Kingdom shape of 911 (63,232 km2 in Cliopatria's table, about 89,000 km2 by the resolver's cells; bbox 114.98-119.65 E, 38.68-41.45 N) stands for the core. Ying and Mo prefectures lie south of it (a 50 km circle at 116.1 E 38.55 N, the researcher's reading, 0 km2 inside the shape): the Liu Rengong page calls them 'Lulong's Ying and Mo' only when Zhu Quanzhong's general captured them in the winter of 900, so drawing them for the whole of 763-897 is a reading; no page dates their joining the circuit. Area check: no page gives an area.

correction.text: the above plus Yichang: Cang Prefecture and Jing Prefecture, taken by Liu Shouwen in 898 (Cangzhou 80 km about 27,800 km2, 3,300 km2 of it inside the Yan shape)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. 'In 898, Liu sent his son Liu Shouwen to attack Yichang's capital Cang Prefecture'; Lu Yanwei fled to Weibo; Liu Rengong made Shouwen acting military governor (the court 'initially refused' a commission). Jing Prefecture is 'Yichang's Jing Prefecture' in the 900 sentence, so it is drawn with Cang (a 40 km circle at 116.27 E 37.7 N, a reading). Yichang held in the name of Liu Rengong's house, so it is drawn as the circuit's land; the alternative reading is a vassal.

correction.text: the Yan core plus Cang Prefecture; Ying, Mo and Jing lost to Zhu Quanzhong in the winter of 900

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. 'Zhang quickly captured Lulong's Ying and Mo' and then 'Yichang's Jing Prefecture' (winter 900); Cang Prefecture, besieged by Ge Congzhou earlier in 900, held under Liu Shouwen. In spring 907 Liu Shouguang seized You Prefecture and captured his father; the page does not say whether Cang left his control then or in 909, so Cang stays in the shape to 908.

correction.text: the Yan core only; Cang Prefecture is contested between Liu Shouguang and Liu Shouwen (drawn by the contest event)

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. 'They fought each other at the Battle of Jisu (in modern Tianjin)' in 909; Liu Shouwen was captured and Liu Shouguang put him under house arrest; Cang was held by Shouwen's son Liu Yanzuo and besieged. The contested zone is carried by the 909 and 910 contest events, so the shape is the core alone.

correction.text: the Yan core plus Cang Prefecture, which fell in 910 when Liu Shouguang 'took Yichang under his control as well'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. 'The city fell in 910, so Liu Shouguang took Yichang under his control as well.' Liu Shouguang had Liu Shouwen killed (no month) and became Prince of Yan in 910; the Yan is claimed in 911.

region.text: the Lulong circuit round You Prefecture (Youzhou), 'near present-day Beijing': the Yan Kingdom shape of 911 stands for the circuit, with Ying (Hejian) and Mo (Renqiu) south of it

ledger.note: 763: Lulong stays with a Yan general. 'Li Huaixian was made military governor (jiedushi) of Lulong Circuit, headquartered in modern Beijing and covering Youzhou, the former Yan core. He was killed in 768, and the circuit remained semi-independent until 913.' Ying and Mo are drawn from 763 as a reading: the pages name them as Lulong's only in 900.

895: Li Keyong installs Liu Rengong. After he 'conquered Lulong', 'in spring 895 Li Keyong formally entered You Prefecture' and left Liu in charge; in summer 895 Emperor Zhaozong formally named Liu military governor of Lulong (Liu had fled to Hedong after Juyong Pass in 893).

region.text: Yichang: Cang Prefecture (Cangzhou) and Jing Prefecture, 'Yichang's Jing Prefecture' in 900 (the Jing circle is a reading)

ledger.note: 898: Yichang taken. 'In 898, Liu sent his son Liu Shouwen to attack Yichang's capital Cang Prefecture'; Lu Yanwei 'abandoned it and fled to Weibo Circuit'; Liu Rengong made Shouwen acting military governor (the court 'initially refused' a formal commission). Cang is on the page; Jing is added from the 900 sentence, so the year is the page's and the region partly a reading.

region.text: Lulong's Ying and Mo prefectures and Yichang's Jing Prefecture (circles at 116.1 E 38.55 N and 116.27 E 37.7 N, a reading)

ledger.note: 900: Zhu Quanzhong's general takes three prefectures. In the winter of 900 'Zhang quickly captured Lulong's Ying and Mo' and then 'Yichang's Jing Prefecture' (Zhang Cunjing); Ge Congzhou had besieged Liu Shouwen at Cang Prefecture earlier in 900 and Cang held. Weibo had already beaten Liu's attack of 899.

region.text: Cang Prefecture (Yichang), held by Liu Shouwen

ledger.note: 909: Liu Shouguang fights his brother over Yichang. 'They fought each other at the Battle of Jisu' (in modern Tianjin); Liu Shouwen was captured and put under house arrest, and Cang, defended by his son Liu Yanzuo, was besieged. The page gives no earlier break; whether Shouwen left his brother's control in 907 is not said.
910: Cang falls. 'The city fell in 910'; Liu Shouguang had Liu Shouwen killed (no month).

region.text: Yichang: Cang Prefecture, 'Liu Shouguang took Yichang under his control as well'

ledger.note: 910: Yichang joins Liu Shouguang's realm. 'The city fell in 910, so Liu Shouguang took Yichang under his control as well.' The Yan Kingdom (911) then holds Yichang with the Lulong core; no dossier exists for Yichang (see notes).

region.text: the Lulong circuit round You Prefecture (Youzhou), 'near present-day Beijing': the Yan Kingdom shape of 911 stands for the circuit, with Cang Prefecture

ledger.note: 911: Liu Shouguang claims the Yan. He seized You Prefecture and arrested his father in 907, became Prince of Yan in 910 (Liu Rengong retired under Later Liang) and 'claims the title of Emperor of Yan' in 911; the Yan is the Yan Kingdom dossier.

wars.name: Li Keyong conquest of Lulong

zones.text: the Lulong circuit round You Prefecture (Youzhou), 'near present-day Beijing': the Yan Kingdom shape of 911 stands for the circuit

wars.outcome: Liu Rengong lost at Juyong Pass in 893; Li Keyong conquered Lulong and entered You Prefecture in spring 895, leaving Liu in charge.
wars.note: The page says 'Li Keyong, having conquered Lulong'; it gives no campaign.

wars.name: Lulong-Zhu Quanzhong war

zones.text: Ying, Mo and Jing prefectures (circles at 116.1 E 38.55 N and 116.27 E 37.7 N, a reading)

wars.outcome: Liu Rengong attacked Weibo in 899 and was beaten; Ge Congzhou besieged Liu Shouwen at Cang Prefecture in 900 without taking it, and Zhang Cunjing took Ying and Mo (Lulong) and Jing (Yichang) in the winter of 900.
wars.note: Zhu Quanzhong was a Tang military governor until 907; the belligerent is listed under the dynasty he founded. Cang held until 910.

wars.name: Liu Shouguang's war on Liu Shouwen (Yichang)
wars.outcome: Liu Shouwen was captured at the Battle of Jisu in 909; Cang, held by his son Liu Yanzuo, fell in 910 and Liu Shouguang took Yichang under his control.
wars.note: Brothers; the page gives no month for the siege or the fall.

certainty.note: Circuit frontiers with no line on the pages.

sources.title: An Lushan rebellion
sources.note: Li Huaixian, Lulong Circuit 763, headquartered in modern Beijing, semi-independent until 913.

sources.title: Liu Rengong
sources.note: 893-901 and 907-914: Li Keyong in You Prefecture, Cang (Yichang) 898 and 910, Ying and Mo (Lulong) and Jing (Yichang) 900, the Battle of Jisu 909, Liu Shouguang.

sources.title: Zhu Ci
sources.note: Opened in the repair for 763-893: Zhu Ci and Zhu Tao helped kill Li Huaixian in 768; Zhu Xicai was acting, then full military governor 768-772 until assassinated; Zhu Ci succeeded in 772 and left for Chang'an in 774 leaving Zhu Tao in acting command of Lulong; the page gives no boundary and records no loss of a Lulong prefecture in the 760s-780s.

notes: New state (Cliopatria lacks it); the Hebei Three Circuits are named in the Tang group's scope. The English Wikipedia has no Lulong Circuit article (Lulong_Circuit returned not found), so wikipedia is null. The history 763-893 rests on the An Lushan page (Li Huaixian 763, killed 768) and the Zhu Ci page opened in the repair (Zhu Xicai 768-772, Zhu Ci 772-774, Zhu Tao acting); Liu Ji, Zhang Zhongwu, Li Kuangwei and the rest are unrecorded here and the Zhu Ci page gives no boundary, so the 763-897 shape is the Yan Kingdom 911 shape plus Ying and Mo as a reading. The yan-kingdom dossier has the Tang as predecessor; Lulong is the nearer one. The 913 end on the An Lushan page is the fall of the Yan, not of Lulong as such. Repair (2026-10-19, after review): the keyframes now carry the ledger. Ying and Mo (the 900 loss) are drawn as Lulong's before 900 (a reading for 763-897, since the Liu Rengong page names them as Lulong's only in 900) and Jing, which the page calls Yichang's, is drawn from 898 with Cang; Cangzhou is drawn 898-908 and 910-911; 909 is the contest of Cang between Liu Shouguang and Liu Shouwen (Jisu 909, the city fell 910). The 898 Cang acquisition stays a gain (Liu Rengong made his son acting governor of Yichang); the alternative, a vassal, is not excluded by the page. Yichang (Lu Yanwei to 898, Liu Shouwen 898-910) has no dossier.
